articles.title: 6 People Have Died From Flu in Connecticut in the Past Month as Cases Rise Nationwide
articles.summary: The flu has hit the U.S. earlier than usual this year. And the virus has already caused six deaths in Connecticut, the state’s department of public health says.
articles.body: The state of Connecticut has already recorded its first flu-related deaths in a flu season that’s hit earlier than is typical. Six people have died since the week ending in Sept. 26, according to new data from the Connecticut Department of Public Health. That week saw the first death, followed by three more in the week ending in October 17 and another two deaths in the week ending in October 24. All six Connecticut residents who’ve died from influenza so far this season were age 55 or older, the department says. There have also been nine COVID deaths since September in the state. “Our hearts are with the families and loved ones of the people that have been lost. These deaths are a sobering reminder that flu can be serious, especially for older adults, and that respiratory virus season is already here,” Dr. Manisha Juthani, commissioner of the Department of Public Health, said in a press release. This time last year, Connecticut had not recorded any flu-related deaths, data show. Flu cases in the state have increased more than 22% since last week and flu-related hospitalizations have increased more than 64%. That increase is similar to what public health experts are seeing in much of the country as the flu arrives earlier in the season than usual this year. An Early Flu Season While no two flu seasons are identical, cases typically pick up around October and last through March, the Mayo Clinic says — though it’s not unusual for cases to linger through May. It’s still too early to know exactly how the 2026-2027 flu season will play out, but experts told TODAY.com they’ve noticed a concerning trend: Flu cases began to tick up as early as August this year. While cases are still low overall, they are growing in much of the U.S., according to data from the Center for Disease Control and Prevention. The most recent CDC data available indicate a nearly 6% increase in positive flu tests in the last week. An early flu season does not necessarily mean a severe flu season, however, the experts said. A newly mutated version of the H1N1 influenza A strain is thought to be responsible for many of the current early flu cases, TODAY.com reported previously, but it’s too early to know whether this version of the virus leads to more serious illness. How to Stay Safe To protect yourself and your family from the flu, you can get a flu vaccine. Experts typically recommend getting your flu vaccine before the end of October. And this year’s vaccine is already available at pharmacies, clinics and doctors’ offices. “If you haven’t gotten it yet for whatever reason, now’s the time to get vaccinated because the flu season is starting a little bit sooner and you need at least two weeks for the vaccine immunity to (reach) protective levels,” Andrew Pekosz, Ph.D., a virologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, told TODAY.com previously. Vaccination is especially important for those considered to be at a higher risk for severe flu complications, which includes older adults, young children and those who are immunocompromised. Getting your vaccine now will also ensure that you’re at a solid level of immunity heading into the winter holiday season. In addition to getting vaccinated, you can also: Wear a well-fitting mask or N95 respirator in crowded indoor settings.Wash your hands frequently.Get tested or test yourself if you develop flu symptoms. And keep in mind that flu isn’t the only illness circulating right now. Both COVID and RSV are also in the mix, and it’s worth making sure you know how to protect yourself from those viruses as well.

articles.title: Targeted drug shrinks tumors in 3 out of 4 patients with advanced breast cancer
articles.summary: A phase 3 clinical trial published in JAMA found trastuzumab rezetecan linked to 73% lower risk of cancer progression or death versus chemotherapy.
articles.body: There may be a promising new treatment on the horizon for advanced breast cancer patients, according to developing research. Researchers are studying the cancer-killing drug trastuzumab rezetecan for those with ERBB2-low metastatic breast cancer, whose tumors have low levels of HER2, a protein that can help cancer cells grow. A phase 3 clinical trial called HORIZON-Breast06 sought to determine whether the drug works better than standard chemotherapy for patients with this cancer type. SHIFT IN CANCER SCREENING GUIDANCE HAS EXPERTS CLASHING OVER NEW GUIDANCE The researchers analyzed 551 female patients across 73 hospitals in China who were randomly assigned to receive either the drug intravenously every three weeks, or the physician’s choice of chemotherapy. The study period lasted from June 2023 to August 2025. The drug significantly delayed cancer progression compared with chemotherapy, giving patients more than a year before their cancer began growing again. The median time without tumor growth was 16.4 months compared to 6.8 months with chemo. FDA APPROVES ONCE-DAILY PILL FOR DEADLY CANCER AFTER PATIENTS' SURVIVAL RATES NEARLY DOUBLE Patients who received trastuzumab rezetecan were 73% less likely to have their cancer worsen or die during the study than patients who received chemotherapy. The drug appeared to delay cancer progression in patients with both hormone receptor-positive and hormone receptor-negative breast cancer. The results were published in JAMA. Tumors shrank in 75.5% of patients who received the drug, compared with 41.2% of those who received chemotherapy. At the 12-month mark, 90.6% of trastuzumab rezetecan patients were alive, compared to 81.4% of chemo patients. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER The authors concluded that trastuzumab rezetecan provided "significant progression-free survival benefit over physician’s choice of chemotherapy in patients with ERBB2-low advanced breast cancer." Loren Rourke, a Texas-based breast surgical oncologist and author in Texas, called the results "incredibly encouraging." "When you're talking about women living with advanced breast cancer, those months matter," Rourke, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital. "They represent more time when the cancer is being held in check and potentially more opportunities to enjoy life without the disease getting worse." What makes these findings especially exciting, according to the oncologist, is that the treatment showed benefits across different types of breast cancer. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "It's another important step forward, and it gives us genuine reason to be hopeful," she said. "A treatment that can keep cancer from progressing for a longer period has the potential to make an enormous difference in a patient's life." While the drug may cause fewer serious lung problems than similar treatments, it was linked to other side effects, including anemia and other blood-related problems. "It's another important step forward, and it gives us genuine reason to be hopeful." Serious side effects occurred in more than 84% of patients who received the new drug, compared with nearly 68% of those who received chemotherapy. Rourke emphasized the importance of considering the side effects, "because more time without cancer progression doesn't automatically mean better quality of life." "We need to better understand the side effects, particularly the significant decreases in blood counts that can lead to fatigue, anemia and increased risk of infection," she said. The researchers acknowledged that toxicity occurred more frequently and often required dose modification, although they said these effects were "generally manageable." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The experts agreed that more research is needed. "As exciting as these findings are, there are still important questions we need to answer," Rourke told Fox News Digital. "We know this treatment delayed cancer progression, but we don't yet know whether it will help patients live longer. That's an important distinction." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It's important to celebrate meaningful progress while making sure we're asking the right questions about what comes next."

articles.title: Judge blocks ‘medically frail’ definition in Medicaid work requirement rule
articles.summary: A federal judge on Thursday blocked President Donald Trump's administration from enforcing a rule that would narrow exceptions to new work requirements for Medicaid recipients with serious medical conditions.
articles.body: A federal judge on Thursday blocked President Donald Trump's administration from enforcing a rule that would narrow exceptions to new work requirements for Medicaid recipients with serious medical conditions. U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns in Boston sided with 25 states and the District of Columbia, which had argued that the new rule would force medically frail people to clear unnecessary hurdles to maintain government-funded health insurance coverage. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, the agency that adopted the rule, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Medicaid, the government health insurance program for low-income Americans, is jointly funded by the federal and state governments. CMS issued the rule in June in order to implement work requirements for Medicaid that were enacted as part of Trump's signature tax and spending measure, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which he signed into law last year. The law requires adults aged 19-64, with a few exceptions, to complete a minimum of 80 hours of work or community engagement activities per month or be enrolled in an education program at least half time to qualify for Medicaid beginning January 1, 2027. CMS’s rule provided guidance to states on how to implement the work requirements, including the law’s exemptions for individuals who are “medically frail or otherwise have special medical needs.” But Stearns said CMS’s rule unlawfully limited who qualifies as “medically frail” by dictating that the exemption only applies if someone’s “physical, mental, or other behavioral health condition significantly impairs the individual’s ability to comply with the community engagement requirement.” “Because enforcement of an unlawful definition of ‘medically frail’ may lead to the disenrollment of otherwise eligible vulnerable individuals relying on Medicaid coverage for continuity of care, the States (and public) face potential for great hardship in the absence of an injunction,” Stearns wrote. The judge was appointed by former President Bill Clinton, a Democrat. While he invalidated that part of the rule, he upheld other provisions that Democratic-led states had also challenged. Among those states were California, Massachusetts and New Jersey, whose attorneys general led the legal challenge.

articles.title: Drake, Ann Michael Maye donate $25k in sports gear to Chelsea students
articles.summary: Patriots quarterback Drake Maye and his wife Ann Michael Maye recently gifted more than $25,000 in sports gear to students of Chelsea High School.
articles.body:
A group of Massachusetts student-athletes just received a surprise from two New England celebrities .

On Wednesday, Oct. 28, New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye and his wife Ann Michael Maye gifted more than $25,000 in sports equipment to students at Chelsea High School. The school's football team and coaches received helmets, shoulder pads, footballs and other gear from Drake Maye himself.

The donation, made through a partnership between the MayeDay Family Foundation and Boston-based nonprofit Good Sports , "marks the launch of Power Up Play, a partnership focused on supporting after-school sports programs at high schools across New England," according to a press release.

"Beyond providing essential equipment, the partnership aims to give young athletes the confidence, resilience and life skills they need to succeed in the classroom, in their communities and in life," the release continues.

Photos: Drake, Ann Michael Maye donate sports gear at Chelsea High School

Launched in March 2026, the MayeDay Family Foundation is a nonprofit founded by Drake and Ann Michael Maye with the goal of providing assistance and support to children and families enduring hardship so that they may achieve a brighter future, according to the foundation's website . The Mayes' foundation will support various programs throughout New England, such as Boston Children's Hospital, as well as in their home state of North Carolina.

Back in May 2026, the charity hosted its first activation, a celebrity softball match at Polar Park in Worcester, Massachusetts. The inaugural game raised over $500,000.

In September 2026, the Mayes donated $15,000 from the foundation to fulfill the Amazon wish lists of all teachers and support specialists at Providence's Alfred Lima Sr. Elementary School.

articles.title: What Is Volume Eating? Dietitian Shares Her No. 1 Strategy for Feeling Full on Fewer Calories
articles.summary: Volume eating can be a useful tool if you’re looking manage your weight, but there are a few things to keep in mind if it’s a practice you’d like to follow.
articles.body: Typical weight loss advice calls for portion control and restriction. But one eating pattern lets you put more food on your plate without sending your calorie count soaring: high-volume eating. “The idea is to focus on foods that provide a lot of volume for relatively few calories, such as vegetables, fruit and broth-based soups,” registered dietitian Erin Palinski-Wade tells TODAY.com. “These foods tend to be naturally rich in water and fiber, which can help you feel satisfied with fewer calories overall.” While this might sound like a plus — a calorie deficit without the mind-consuming hunger — there are some factors you’ll want to keep in mind, says Palinski-Wade. What Is Volume Eating for Weight Loss? “I like to think of it as a strategy for building more satisfying meals rather than another restrictive diet,” says Palinski-Wade. It’s especially helpful if you’re trying to lose or maintain a certain weight but struggle to feel full and satisfied, she adds. Rather than slashing your portions sizes or completely cutting out higher calorie foods you love, you can change some of the foods you eat so that you can eat larger, more filling portions of them for fewer calories. This way, you leave your meals feeling satiated and, in some cases, you might find you have leftover or unused calories in the “bank” for the occasional higher-calorie food or treat. The research shows this can work, too. One analysis that looked at 31 studies found that reducing the calorie or energy density in one’s meals helped to reduce overall caloric intake. “Other research has found that people eating lower energy-density diets could actually consume 1-2 pounds more food per day while taking in fewer calories and losing more weight over six months,” adds Palinski-Wade. Who Should Consider Volume Eating? People looking to manage their weight, whether losing it or maintaining it, might find volume eating to be a useful tool. It can feel discouraging to reduce the amount of food on your plate when you’re used to a certain amount and miss that feeling of comfortable fullness at the end of your meals. “Choosing more high-volume foods may make it easier to manage calories without feeling deprived,” says Palinksi-Wade. Even if weight management isn’t your goal, there are still benefits to volume eating. Palinksi-Wade says those of us who eat out of habit, boredom or tend to emotionally eat can turn to this practice for the familiar and soothing sensation of chewing and eating. “And for the many Americans who aren’t eating enough fruits and vegetables,” she adds, “focusing on adding more volume through produce can be a great way to improve overall nutrition.” Who Should Avoid Volume Eating? While volume eating is useful for some, Palinski-Wade urges caution for a few different groups To start, for someone with a current or past eating disorder, including binge eating disorder, “this approach may reinforce an unhealthy relationship with food or feelings of fullness,” she says. If you notice your focus shifts from seeking a feeling of satisfaction after a meal to consuming the largest amount of food for the fewest possible calories while ignoring your body’s hunger and fullness cues, volume eating isn’t for you. “People with certain digestive conditions, such as IBS, Crohn’s disease or other forms of inflammatory bowel disease, may also struggle with large amounts of high-fiber foods,” says Palinski-Wade. “Anyone with a history of bowel obstruction, bowel surgery, or difficulty absorbing nutrients should speak with their healthcare provider before significantly increasing fiber intake.” Anyone on a GLP-1 will also want to be cautious. Eating large portions, even if they’re low in calories, can worsen nausea and gut discomfort since these medications slow digestion. “For these individuals, prioritizing protein and nutrient-dense foods in smaller portions is generally a better strategy,” says Palinski-Wade. Finally, anyone who burns calories at a fast rate should avoid volume eating. Think athletes, or highly active gym-goers, runners or swimmers, will find it hard to consume enough energy from high amounts of low-calorie foods to support their movement, performance and recovery. How to Practice Volume Eating Prioritize Foods High in Water and Fiber Think foods like leafy greens, cucumbers, peppers, berries and watermelon, says Palinkski-Wade. These foods take up a lot of space on your plate (and in your stomach) without adding significantly to your overall daily caloric intake. When It Doubt, Try Soup One strategy, she suggests, is to start your meals with a broth-based soup to make your meals more satisfying for fewer calories. “One study found that people who ate two servings of low-calorie-density soup each day lost 50% more weight over a year than those consuming the same calories from snack foods,” says Palinski-Wade. “And including a wider variety of low-energy-density foods may also help improve overall diet quality.” Keep in Mind When Volume Eating… Volume eating can impact your hunger and fullness cues in ways that are both beneficial and detrimental. On the upside, you’ll experience the familiar sensation of comfortable fullness from lower-calorie foods as they take up space in your stomach. “That physical stretching sends signals to your brain that you’re getting full, which may help you feel satisfied while consuming fewer calories,” Palinski-Wade says. However, volume alone shouldn’t be your priority. It might cause you to lose sight of balanced meals. Your focus for every meal should be consuming adequate amounts of protein, carbs, healthy fats, fiber, vitamins and minerals. Eating all the essential macro and micronutrients are just as important for satiety. “The goal should be to feel comfortably satisfied after eating, not to feel as physically full as possible,” says Palinksi-Wade. While you’re eating, check in with yourself. Halfway through your meal, pause and ask yourself whether you’re still hungry or eating because the food is in front of you. “It can take about 20 minutes for your brain to fully register feelings of fullness,” she says. “Slowing down and checking in with yourself during a meal can make a big difference.” If 20 minutes after your meal you find you’re still hungry, go ahead and eat more.

articles.title: Patrick Stewart Died After Battling Alzheimer’s and Lewy Body Dementia. What to Know
articles.summary: Legendary actor Patrick Stewart passed away this week after a brief experience with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia. What to know about the conditions.
articles.body: Legendary actor Patrick Stewart passed away at age 86 this week. His death came after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” according to a statement posted on Stewart’s official Instagram page. Stewart, known for iconic roles such as Captain Jean-Luc Picard and Professor Charles Xavier, had not publicly disclosed his diagnoses prior to his death. Both Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia are progressive neurodegenerative conditions causing symptoms such as issues with memory, thinking and attention. While Lewy body dementia may be misdiagnosed as Alzheimer’s, they can also occur together. What Is Lewy Body Dementia? Lewy body dementia is the second most common form of degenerative dementia, TODAY.com explained previously, with Alzheimer’s disease being the first. When someone is diagnosed with both Alzheimer’s and Lewy body dementia, it’s called “mixed dementia,” according to the Alzheimer’s Association. The condition occurs when a buildup of protein deposits, called Lewy bodies, form in the brain’s nerve cells. This specifically affects areas of the brain involved in regulating our movement, thinking and memory, the Mayo Clinic explains. Many people became familiar with Lewy body dementia after comedian and actor Robin Williams’ death put it into the spotlight. And earlier this year Ted Turner died following a Lewy body dementia diagnosis. Overlap in Alzheimer’s and Lewy Body Dementia Symptoms It can sometimes be challenging to diagnose these conditions because there is overlap in some symptoms — and they can occur together. Like Lewy body dementia, Alzheimer’s is caused by the buildup of protein “plaques,” leading to changes in cognition, particularly memory. And in both cases, the diseases are progressive, meaning symptoms will get worse over time. However, the Mayo Clinic notes that those with Lewy body dementia may also experience other characteristic symptoms, such as: HallucinationsMovement changes, including signs of Parkinson’s diseaseSleep disturbances, such as acting out dreamsPoor regulation of bodily functions manifesting as drops in blood pressure or dizziness, for instance Not everyone with Lewy body dementia will notice their disease progressing in the same way. There is currently no cure for Lewy body dementia and the disease is complex, but there are some medications that can be helpful in managing some of the symptoms. After a diagnosis of Lewy body dementia, people live an average of five to eight years, the Cleveland Clinic notes.

articles.title: FOX News Media teams up with Breast Cancer Research Foundation
articles.summary: At a Fox News panel with the Breast Cancer Research Foundation, Kat Timpf discussed her Stage 0 diagnosis, self-advocacy and rising cancer rates in younger women.
articles.body: FOX News Media teamed up with the Breast Cancer Research Foundation (BCRF) Thursday for a special panel highlighting advances in breast cancer research and treatment while urging women to take an active role in their healthcare. The event, held at Fox News headquarters in New York City during Breast Cancer Awareness Month, featured Kat Timpf, the "Gutfeld!" co-host and breast cancer survivor, alongside Dr. Priya Malhotra, director of research impact at BCRF. Speaking with Fox News Digital after the panel, Timpf emphasized that while breast cancer awareness is widespread, misconceptions about the disease persist and may discourage people from asking important questions about their health. LARRY FITZGERALD Q&A: NFL ICON TALKS BREAST CANCER AWARENESS FOR HIS LATE MOTHER, FRIENDSHIP WITH JOHN MCCAIN "There is also so much that people don’t know. It can happen at any age, without genetic markers. I would know that," Timpf told Fox News Digital. "Talking about it is always helpful because it removes a lot of the stigma, and it makes you feel like you can ask these questions to your doctor." Timpf was diagnosed with Stage 0 ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) in February 2025, just 15 hours before giving birth to her first child. She announced the news on social media days later, writing what she called an "unconventional birth announcement." "Last week, I welcomed my first child into the world. About fifteen hours before I went into labor, I was diagnosed with breast cancer," Timpf wrote on X at the time. "Now, before you worry, my doctor says it’s stage 0 and is confident that it almost certainly hasn’t spread. Or, as I’ve explained to the few people I’ve managed to tell about it so far: Don’t freak out. It’s just, like, a LITTLE bit of cancer." VANESSA TRUMP REVEALS BREAST CANCER DIAGNOSIS IN EMOTIONAL STATEMENT: 'I AM STAYING FOCUSED AND HOPEFUL' Throughout her breast cancer experience, Timpf leaned on her signature humor, a coping mechanism she said helped her through some of the most difficult moments of her diagnosis and recovery. "Humor is how I've gotten through every hard thing that's ever happened to me," Timpf said. "I was making jokes the day I was diagnosed about getting huge replacement [implants] and stuff like that. That's just how I do things because I feel like when you say that you can't joke about a subject, you're giving it even more power over you than it already has. "For me, making jokes about a subject is a way to instead feel power over the things that are threatening to take you down." TRUMP'S CHIEF OF STAFF ALMOST SKIPPED SCREENING THAT DETECTED AGGRESSIVE CANCER Timpf's central message to women was to take an active role in their healthcare, stay on top of recommended screenings and speak up when something doesn't feel right. "Your own health is up to you. So, you have to make sure you pay attention and ask your doctor questions," Timpf said. "Don't think it can't happen to you because I thought that, and I was wrong." Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women in the U.S. and worldwide, with approximately one in eight U.S. women expected to develop invasive breast cancer during their lifetime, according to the Breast Cancer Research Foundation. LINDA PERRY SAYS SHE WAS FEELING HEALTHY WHEN DOCTORS DISCOVERED ‘ANGRY’ CANCER BY CHANCE While breast cancer has historically been more commonly diagnosed in older women, rates are rising among younger women, including those under 40, before routine mammograms are generally recommended for women at average risk. Dr. Malhotra emphasized that while breast cancer diagnoses in younger women account for a relatively small share of cases, the impact is profound. "Incidence of breast cancer is rising in younger women," Dr. Malhotra told Fox News Digital. "Maybe 10% of breast cancers are in younger women," she added. "But still, if you're one of the 10%, it's crushing." ‘X-MEN’ STAR TYLER MANE SAYS WIFE ‘SAVED MY LIFE’ AFTER SEEMINGLY HARMLESS LUMP LED TO BREAST CANCER DIAGNOSIS Dr. Malhotra, who previously served on the faculty at Georgetown University, now works at BCRF to help advance breast cancer research. She highlighted the growing number of targeted treatments developed in recent decades. "In 1977, we had one targeted treatment for breast cancer. Twenty years later, we had two," Dr. Malhotra explained. "Fast forward to today, we have over 30 targeted treatments, 19 in the last decade alone. So, it’s moving very quickly, and we're proud to say that our investigators are involved in all of those, getting them across the finish line." She also stressed the importance of recognizing changes in one's body and speaking up during medical appointments. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "My biggest thing is to know your body because if you feel that something is out of whack — even if you think it's minor — it’s worth it to talk to your doctor about," Dr. Malhotra said.

articles.title: Ceredigion heart attack patient had 140-mile round hospital trip
articles.summary: Charles Swift faced a 140-mile round trip to get to a hospital, but had to drive himself.
articles.body:
An 83-year-old recovering cancer patient who has suffered two heart attacks was forced to drive himself on a four-hour round trip for medical tests.

Charles Swift was referred to Withybush Hospital in Haverfordwest, Pembrokeshire, for tests on his heart in August - he lives in Borth, Ceredigion - which is 70 miles away.

He made inquiries about getting non-emergency transport but was refused by a call handler from the Welsh Ambulance Services Trust (WAST) when he told them he owned a car.

"I can't understand why pensioners have to run about in their own car," he said.

WAST said it was not always able to meet the increasing demand for transport, and changes were underway to improve the service.

Swift, who has been treated for three types of cancer and has had two heart attacks, said when he rang hospital taxis, he was asked if he could walk, climb stairs and owned a car.

When he replied yes to all three, he said he was told: "You'll have to use that then.

"I don't understand. What's the difference if you've got a car or not? I'm 83. It's not a good journey to do. It was tiring."

On another occasion, Swift was told on a Friday afternoon that his hospital transport for an appointment in Haverfordwest on the Monday had been cancelled, leading him to cancel the appointment.

When he got hospital transport for a subsequent appointment, he said it was "very pleasant, no problem at all".

Hywel Dda University Health Board's website says patients travelling to and from hospital are normally expected to organise their own transport.

When that is not possible, some patients could be eligible for non-emergency patient transport provided by the Welsh Ambulance Service, but must meet eligibility criteria.

This includes receiving regular dialysis or cancer treatment, needing a stretcher or oxygen or needing to travel in their own wheelchair.

Public transport is not a realistic option as trains from Borth to Haverfordwest take a minimum of three-and-a-half hours in each direction.

Councillors in Ceredigion have made calls for better hospital transport system in rural areas.

One of them, Hugh Hughes, met Swift shortly after his first appointment when the health board wanted him to go back for a second one.

He said: "He was distraught. He didn't know how he was going to manage it. He was absolutely exhausted after the first experience."

After Swift's initial request for transport, the ambulance service reviewed his phone call.

According to Mark Harris, WAST's assistant director of operations, the transport would not have been refused if the service had more information.

"We've changed our processes now, and we've put some training out to our call taking team, so when Mr Swift rings again, he'll get a different answer," he said.

Harris said the demand for transport and the distances travelled to appointments were increasing, placing a strain on resources, which could lead to the cancellation of transport.

"We are seeing an increase in the volume of journeys we have to cancel where the demand exceeds our available resource," he said. "So we will get occasions where we have more work than we can fit on our vehicles within a day [and] we're in the middle of a significant improvement programme now to address that."

The councillors and voluntary organisations involved in patient transport have said that, even when a patient gets transport, bookings are frequently cancelled the day before the appointment.

Hughes said: "We've got a very good hospital in Bronglais just on our doorstep yet many of the services seem to be migrating further south.

"We've got to accept there will be occasions where you have to travel. But this seems to be becoming far more prevalent."

Dolen Teifi - a community transport service based in Llandysul - has 42 vehicles and 160 volunteer drivers covering Ceredigion and Carmarthenshire.

The charity's manager Rod Bowen said drivers make about 50 journeys to hospital appointments each week and had noticed that the ambulance service's capacity "has been stretched".

While the non-emergency ambulance service is free, Dolen Teifi charges an average of 57p a mile to partly cover its costs.

"The demand for hospital appointments has gone up," added Bowen.

Bowen said the charity had taken 145 calls in the past two months when hospital transport had been cancelled the day before an appointment, and it was able to help in about a third of cases.

"We've been able to fill that gap, and it's quite an important gap to fill because basically that means the person can actually get to the hospital for their appointment," he added.

"We've seen a huge increase of people having to travel past their main hospital door to a hospital that could be anything up to 40 to 50 miles away."

Bowen also said longer journeys for appointments were more common and older patients were "not really comfortable" driving to hospitals in unfamiliar areas.

Hughes said the health board and the ambulance service needed to work together as people were "falling through the net and are not getting the transport they need".

Andrew Carruthers, chief operating officer at Hywel Dda health board, said the board covered a large rural area and it was "aware of the challenges that some of our patients face especially when they have to travel longer distances to access specialist treatment."

He added it worked closely with WAST, and it would raise concerns to see how "transport options available for our patients" could be improved.

articles.title: Deadly disease sparks new CDC rule for US-bound flyers as major airlines seek delay
articles.summary: U.S. and international airlines are urging the CDC to delay its Nov. 3 Ebola travel form requirement affecting all U.S.-bound passengers. An infectious disease expert shares insights.
articles.body: Major U.S. and international airline groups are pushing back against a new Ebola-related travel requirement that will affect millions of people flying into the United States. Beginning Nov. 3, all passengers on international flights to the U.S. will have to confirm that they have not been in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) during the previous 21 days, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The requirement applies to everyone flying into or connecting through the U.S. — including American citizens, green card holders and airline crew members, the CDC said. US ISSUES URGENT TRAVEL WARNING AS DEADLY EBOLA OUTBREAK SPREADS OVERSEAS Travelers will have to complete a paper or digital statement before boarding, even if they have never visited the DRC. Airlines must collect the forms and keep them for at least 42 days after the flight arrives in the U.S., according to the CDC. Airlines for America (A4A), which represents major carriers including American, Delta, Southwest, United and JetBlue, is asking the CDC to reconsider the requirement and give airlines more time to prepare, according to an Oct. 26 letter provided to Fox News Digital. The group said it supports the CDC's public health goals but argued that the new requirement is too broad and is being introduced too quickly. "We have to ensure that this does not cross borders." A4A asked the government for a "more proportionate and measured U.S. response" focused more closely on affected areas and travelers who have recently been there. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The group also asked for the Nov. 3 start date to be delayed. "Changes to check-in systems, digital signatures, station procedures and training cannot readily be completed in the allotted time," A4A wrote. Dr. Tyler Evans, a California-based infectious disease physician and CEO of Wellness Equity Alliance, told Fox News Digital, "This was a step in the right direction, given the fact that we really do have to take this seriously. We have to ensure that this does not cross borders." He added, "This is the second-largest outbreak of Ebola in history. So this is very serious." The International Air Transport Association (IATA), which represents more than 370 airlines around the world, has also asked the CDC to reconsider the requirement, Reuters reported. "This is the second-largest outbreak of Ebola in history." "It is unreasonable for the U.S. government to require all airlines serving the U.S. market to modify their procedures to accommodate the collection of attestations from each individual (passenger and crew) flying to the United States in less than two weeks," IATA wrote in a letter, according to Reuters. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES A4A is also asking the CDC to exempt airline crew members, arguing that existing aviation documents already contain information about crews and their travel. The group has requested an exemption for U.S. military passenger charters as well, saying the military already tracks service members' health, safety and whereabouts. articles.title: BOBBY BURACK: Online hate is winning, from Pat McAfee to everyday Americans and young children
articles.summary: Pat McAfee, Clay Travis and a doctor with 200,000 X followers reveal how online hate and death threats are driving public figures off platforms.
articles.body: Imagine a place where people are twice as likely to say something negative about you as something positive. A place where they feel free to insult you in ways they would never attempt in person. A place where they are incentivized, sometimes financially, for saying things about you that are untrue. Social media is that place. Online hate has received renewed attention in recent weeks. Most notably, ESPN commentator Pat McAfee cited online remarks, lies, and death threats when explaining why he felt unsafe at a Utah college campus last week. He said people frequently tell him they want to "Kirk" him, a reference to the assassination of political activist Charlie Kirk. BOBBY BURACK: JUSTIN TUCKER SIGNING EXPOSES SPORTS MEDIA’S SELECTIVE OUTRAGE OVER NFL MISCONDUCT OutKick founder Clay Travis has described receiving similar messages almost every day. McAfee and Travis are not alone. Anyone with a public platform or a controversial opinion has likely faced an online barrage of abuse, often more than once. In my experience, negative comments outnumber positive ones by an even wider margin than the nearly two-to-one ratio University of Minnesota researchers found. The mental health consequences are not only measurable but notable. In a 2025 experiment involving 128 adults, participants exposed to negative social media comments recorded anxiety scores of 2.42, compared with 1.77 among those who saw neutral comments and 1.55 among those who saw positive comments. Their pleasant mood scores also fell to 2.37, compared with 3.05 after neutral comments and 3.25 after positive comments. Translation: their moods were tied to what people say to them and about them online. A separate meta-analysis found that adolescents who experienced cyberbullying had 2.73 times the odds of developing depression as those who had not. The numbers are concerning. Social media hostility can cause serious distress, from children and teenagers to professional athletes and public figures. Jesse Morse, M.D., built an X following of more than 200,000 people by providing injury analysis on NFL players. His account generated enough engagement to qualify for monetization. Last week, he said he had "retired" from the role because of the relentless negativity. "My reputation is not worth it. I get so much hate. It’s just not worth it anymore," Morse wrote. Maybe it is not worth it. That is for you to decide. But the people spreading the hate are not worth it. They are not worth acknowledging. They are mere strangers to you. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Think about the logic of allowing someone who does not know you to determine your mood. If someone criticized a movie but admitted they had watched only a few seconds, you would dismiss the review immediately. You wouldn't give credibility to someone judging an entire film from an incomplete sample. Social media criticism is often no different. People are far more complex than films. And yet, most users who insult you are responding to a single post, comment or moment. They are judging your character based on one short scene. Their opinion is not credible. It only becomes so if you decide to make it credible. Social media also distorts public opinion. Studies show that negative content is overrepresented because it attracts more engagement and spreads more widely. In return, positive reactions are quieter and less visible. The online response is not a representative sample of the real world. In previous generations, most people had no idea what strangers thought of them. Strangers had no way to announce their opinions directly. Now they do. That is the only thing that has changed. Their opinions have not become more informed, accurate or important simply because technology can deliver them to your phone. So stop treating them as if they have. Do not let people who do not know you define you. Do not let the most unreasonable and uninformed people defeat you. Ignore them. Turn off your mentions. Restrict replies. Disable public comments. Delete social media, if you wish. The moment you stop giving strangers access to your attention, you render them powerless. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Unless a troll is a direct threat to what matters most in your life — friends, family, career, health, safety — they should have no place in your mind. Hate is lonely when no one notices it.

articles.title: Ric Flair Gives Health Update After Bloody Fall: 'I Will Be Okay'
articles.summary: The WWE legend thanked fans and hospital staff after suffering head and eye injuries in Tampa.
articles.body:
The 77-year-old wrestling legend took to social media Saturday (Oct. 24) to reassure fans that he's recovering at home following Friday's incident. Flair shared a photo of himself sitting in a chair with a circular bandage covering his right eye.

"Thank you all for the messages and prayers! I will get back to you all individually as I get stronger," Flair wrote. "Thank you to Tampa General Hospital staff and doctors that put up with me until 4:30 a.m. I appreciate you all and thank you for everything you did. I am focused on my healing and recovery right now, and I will be okay."

According to TMZ, Flair was at Wagamama in Tampa on Friday morning when he got up from the bar, leaving his phone and drink behind, and walked across the street.

The WWE Hall of Famer reportedly fell shortly afterward, suffering cuts to his head and the area surrounding his eye. Emergency responders arrived at the scene and transported Flair to a nearby hospital by ambulance.

His daughter, WWE star Charlotte Flair, provided an update shortly after the fall, letting fans know her father was stable while sharing a joke he made to his doctor.

"Not my dad telling the doctor he fell bc of warrior dropping him on his head… (ps: he's going to be ok)," she wrote on X, referencing her father's history with the late Ultimate Warrior.

Flair's son-in-law, wrestling podcaster Conrad Thompson, later confirmed that the Nature Boy had returned home.

The incident occurred just hours after Flair revealed that he was dealing with a blood clot in his leg, forcing him to cancel a scheduled appearance at Washington State Horror Con in Seattle.

"Blood clots are extremely serious and can be life-threatening. We have seen this recently with Jalen Hurts and the complications involving blood clots in his lungs," Flair wrote in his earlier announcement. "It is a reminder that this is not something to take lightly, and I must follow medical advice."

Flair explained that doctors had restricted his travel to trips lasting no more than three to four hours. He also revealed plans to undergo a procedure to address the affected vein.

articles.title: Daylight saving time is ending: Doctor breaks down 6 ways to protect your sleep and health
articles.summary: Turning the clocks back disrupts sleep and mood. Dr. John La Puma shares six tips, from schedule shifts to chamomile tea and limiting screen time.
articles.body: Turning the clocks back at the end of daylight saving time has been linked to trouble falling and staying asleep, while ongoing sleep loss can take a toll on health. While some research has suggested that the fall time change could have some cardiovascular benefits, the abrupt loss of evening sunlight can suppress serotonin and melatonin production, which can lead to a depressed mood, according to Dr. John La Puma, a California physician and expert in nature-based medicine. The body’s internal clock does not automatically follow the clock on the wall, La Puma noted. THE DAYTIME HABIT THAT COULD TRANSFORM YOUR SLEEP, ACCORDING TO NEW STUDY "When the clocks change, your body clock is still on the old time," he told Fox News Digital, pointing out some common effects people may notice. "So, for about a week, you wake up an hour early. You get hungry early. You feel sleepy early. It gets dark by five. Afternoon light goes away. You get months of short days. … You need coffee just to feel human. It's not great." Making small adjustments to your routine after the time change could help ease the transition, the doctor said. No. 1: Make small schedule shifts With clocks turning back overnight Saturday, people can begin moving bedtime, meals and wake-up time later in small increments on Friday, according to La Puma. "So, you move your day later in small steps," he advised. "You move your bedtime and meals the same 15 minutes each time." DOCTOR REVEALS 4 HIDDEN HEALTH RISKS OF SPENDING TOO MUCH TIME INDOORS For someone who normally goes to bed at 10 p.m., that could mean 10:15 p.m. Friday and 10:30 p.m. Saturday, before the clocks change. Wake-up times and meals can shift by the same increments as schedules allow. No. 2: Don't spend the ‘extra hour’ on a late night Since the time change falls on Halloween, Dr. Saema Tahir, a sleep medicine doctor in New York City, cautioned against staying up late and drinking, operating under the assumption that the extra hour covers it. "Keep alcohol moderate, finish drinking a few hours before bed and avoid caffeine after early afternoon," she advised. "Alcohol makes you drowsy at first but breaks up sleep in the second half of the night. Caffeine stays in your system for hours. Together, they can leave you more tired on Sunday than you would be with no time change at all." No. 3: Get outside at the right time La Puma also emphasized the importance of being intentional about outdoor exposure. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "You want to get outside at the right minutes, at the time of day and in the right place if you can," he advised, specifically recommending getting outside each afternoon later in the day. "Late-day daylight is different than morning daylight. Late-day daylight tells your body the day is running long, and it shifts later," he said. Once you've adjusted to the time change, Tahir recommends getting outdoor light within an hour of waking every day through the winter. "Light is the strongest signal the body clock gets," she told Fox News Digital. "Evening light pushes it later, which is the direction you need to go for 'fall back.' Morning light keeps it stable over the darker months and supports mood and daytime alertness." No. 4: Create a wind-down routine Choosing a relaxing activity that signals bedtime is approaching can help to promote a consistent sleep schedule. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP La Puma suggests choosing a relaxing bedtime ritual, such as working in a paper workbook, sipping chamomile tea, taking a bath or using aromatherapy, options he outlines in his book, "Indoor Epidemic." "Very specific things that tell your brain and body, 'I'm winding down so I can go to sleep.'" No. 5: Avoid caffeine and screens Other tips include limiting caffeine after noon and stopping screen time at least an hour before bedtime. La Puma warned that light from the screen can suppress melatonin, the hormone that helps signal it is time to sleep. Even using night mode may not fully prevent that effect. No. 6: Keep a consistent schedule after the change Once the clocks change, it’s important to maintain a regular wake-up time, including on weekends, La Puma said. "Pick one wake-up time and keep it every day, weekdays and weekends." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER La Puma cited an eight-year study of about 60,000 people that linked consistent sleep and wake times to a 19% lower risk of death. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "So, sleep and wake times have important effects on heart attack, stroke and cardiovascular mortality," he said. Anyone experiencing persistent trouble falling or staying asleep, frequent daytime fatigue or sleep loss that interferes with daily activities should contact a healthcare provider, according to the National Institutes of Health.

articles.title: Capotamentos em Buíque deixam três mortos em menos de 24 horas | G1
articles.standfirst: Acidentes aconteceram na zona rural do município. Entre as vítimas estão um homem de 46 anos e uma adolescente de 17 anos, pai e filha.
articles.summary: Três pessoas morreram em acidentes em dois acidentes em menos de 24 horas em Buíque, incluindo pai e filha grávida.
articles.body:
Dois acidentes de trânsito registrados em menos de 24 horas deixaram três pessoas mortas em Buíque , no Agreste de Pernambuco. As ocorrências envolveram o capotamento de um carro, na tarde da quinta-feira (29), na estrada do Vale do Catimbau, e de um caminhão, na manhã desta sexta-feira (30), às margens da PE-250.

No primeiro acidente, morreram Geraldo Torres, de 46 anos, e a filha dele, Jennifer Torres, de 17 anos, que estava grávida. Já no capotamento do caminhão, uma pessoa morreu e outras duas ficaram feridas. As circunstâncias dos dois acidentes são investigadas.

Pai e filha mortos em acidente na Zona Rural de Buíque — Foto: Reprodução

O primeiro acidente aconteceu na tarde da quinta-feira (29), em uma estrada do Vale do Catimbau, na zona rural de Buíque. Geraldo Torres dirigia um carro quando um dos pneus estourou, fazendo com que ele perdesse o controle da direção. O veículo capotou.

O motorista e a filha, Jennifer Torres, que também estava no carro, morreram no local. O Instituto de Criminalística (IC) realizou a perícia, e os corpos foram encaminhados ao Instituto de Medicina Legal (IML) de Caruaru.

Em nota, a Polícia Civil informou que registrou a ocorrência por meio da Delegacia de Buíque. Um inquérito foi instaurado para investigar as circunstâncias do acidente.

Caminhão capotou na estrada da vila Guanumbi, em Buíque — Foto: Reprodução

O segundo acidente aconteceu na manhã desta sexta-feira (30), às margens da PE-250, caminho para a Vila Guanumbi, na zona rural de Buíque. Um caminhão carregado com material de construção capotou e três pessoas foram apontadas pelo Corpo de Bombeiros como envolvidas na ocorrência.

De acordo com o Corpo de Bombeiros, duas vítimas já haviam sido socorridas por populares e por uma ambulância do município quando as equipes chegaram ao local. A terceira foi encontrada presa sob a carroceria do caminhão, sem sinais vitais. Os nomes das vítimas não foram divulgados.

A Prefeitura de Buíque informou que uma vítima das vítimas foi retirada do veículo por populares e encaminhada ao Hospital Municipal. Após receber os primeiros atendimentos e ser estabilizada, ela foi transferida para o Hospital da Restauração, no Recife. Até a última atualização, não havia informações sobre o estado de saúde da vítima.

Segundo a Secretaria de Saúde do município, não houve registro de entrada no hospital municipal da terceira pessoa que teria se envolvido no acidente e teria sido resgata por populares.

O Corpo de Bombeiros acionou a Polícia Militar e o Instituto de Criminalística para os procedimentos necessários. O corpo da vítima que morreu foi retirado pela equipe da corporação.

articles.title: Dono de parque de vaquejada é morto pelo filho em Petrolina | G1
articles.standfirst: Antônio Alcântara, de 57 anos, foi atacado na residência da filha. Uma jovem de 28 anos acabou ferida no peito e levada ao Hospital Universitário. A Polícia Civil apura o assassinato.
articles.summary: Dono de parque de vaquejada morto em Petrolina, Antônio Alcântara foi atacado na casa da filha; a polícia investiga o crime que também feriu uma jovem de 28 anos.
articles.body:
Filho mata pai a tiros no n-4 do perímetro irrigado Nilo Coelho. — Foto: Renata Alves/ TV Grande Rio

O dono de um parque de vaquejada foi morto na noite de quinta-feira (29) , em Petrolina , no Sertão de Pernambuco. A vítima é Antônio Alcântara do Nascimento, de 57 anos, conhecido como 'Sabugo'. O crime aconteceu, após um desentendimento familiar, na casa da filha de Antônio localizada no núcleo 4 do perímetro irrigado Nilo Coelho, na Zona Rural.

O autor dos disparos foi identificado apenas como George, filho de Antônio, de 37 anos.

Durante a confusão, uma mulher de 28 anos, identificada como Lauane Oliveira, também foi atingida por um tiro no peito. Ela foi socorrida e levada ao Hospital Universitário (HU). Até a última atualização desta reportagem, não havia informações sobre o estado de saúde dela.

A Delegacia de Homicídios de Petrolina registrou o homicídio consumado e a tentativa de homicídio e segue em diligências até o esclarecimento do caso.

articles.title: Dia Mundial do AVC: HSJ promove ação e reforça a importância de agir rápido | G1
articles.standfirst: Atividade realizada com pacientes destaca os sinais de alerta, o papel da Unidade de AVC e a continuidade dos cuidados após a alta hospitalar
articles.summary: Atividade realizada com pacientes destaca os sinais de alerta, o papel da Unidade de AVC e a continuidade dos cuidados após a alta hospitalar
articles.body:
O reconhecimento dos primeiros sinais e a rapidez na busca por atendimento médico podem fazer a diferença entre a recuperação e a ocorrência de sequelas graves. No Dia Mundial do Acidente Vascular Cerebral (AVC), lembrado nesta quinta-feira, 29 de outubro, o Hospital São José, de Criciúma, realizou uma ação especial de conscientização com os pacientes, reforçando as orientações sobre a identificação dos sintomas, a importância do atendimento de emergência e os cuidados necessários para prevenir novos episódios.

A iniciativa também destaca o trabalho desenvolvido pela Unidade de AVC do hospital, referência no atendimento de pacientes da região Sul de Santa Catarina. A estrutura oferece assistência especializada desde a fase aguda da doença, com investigação das possíveis causas e definição das condutas necessárias para o tratamento e a prevenção de recorrências.

De acordo com a neurologista Dra. Isabel Rampinelli, a data é uma oportunidade para ampliar o conhecimento da população sobre uma doença que está entre as principais causas de morte e incapacidade. “Saber reconhecer os principais sintomas, identificar o início do quadro e entender como procurar ajuda é fundamental para reduzir tanto a mortalidade quanto as sequelas”, explica.

A médica ressalta que os sinais podem surgir de forma repentina e nem sempre se manifestam da mesma maneira. Fraqueza ou dormência em um lado do corpo, boca torta, fala arrastada, alterações na visão, tontura e perda de equilíbrio estão entre os principais alertas.

“Qualquer sinal de anormalidade deve ser levado a sério. A orientação é ligar para o SAMU, pelo número 192, informar os sintomas e buscar atendimento de emergência”, reforça a neurologista.

A Unidade de AVC do Hospital São José oferece assistência especializada a pacientes da região Sul de Santa Catarina — Foto: Divulgação/Hospital São José

O AVC ocorre quando o fluxo sanguíneo para uma parte do cérebro é interrompido ou quando há o rompimento de um vaso sanguíneo. Sem receber oxigênio adequadamente, as células cerebrais podem sofrer danos, que se agravam à medida que o tempo passa.

Por isso, o atendimento rápido é determinante para avaliar as possibilidades de tratamento. Nos casos de AVC isquêmico, alguns tratamentos para dissolver o coágulo podem ser indicados em uma janela de até quatro horas e meia após o início dos sintomas, conforme a avaliação médica e os critérios clínicos. Quanto antes o paciente chegar ao serviço de referência, maiores podem ser as chances de um tratamento bem-sucedido.

“No AVC, o tempo é vida. Quanto mais tempo o cérebro fica sem receber oxigênio adequadamente, maior pode ser o dano. Quanto antes oferecemos o tratamento, maior a chance de sucesso e menor o risco de sequelas”, destaca Dra. Isabel.

No Hospital São José, o atendimento inclui a avaliação da condição aguda, a investigação das possíveis causas do AVC e o planejamento dos cuidados necessários para reduzir o risco de um novo episódio. O hospital é habilitado pelo Ministério da Saúde como Centro de Atendimento de Urgência aos Pacientes com AVC. O trabalho desenvolvido pela instituição também já recebeu reconhecimento internacional. A instituição conquistou o selo Diamante do Angels Awards, a mais alta categoria da premiação, que reconhece a qualidade da assistência e a agilidade no atendimento aos pacientes com AVC.

A neurologista Dra. Isabel Rampinelli destaca que reconhecer os sintomas do AVC e procurar atendimento imediato pode reduzir o risco de sequelas — Foto: Divulgação/Hospital São José

Além do atendimento rápido e especializado, a continuidade dos cuidados após a alta hospitalar também é importante para prevenir novos episódios. Seguir corretamente as orientações médicas, utilizar os medicamentos prescritos e manter o acompanhamento de saúde são medidas que contribuem para reduzir o risco de recorrência.

A adesão ao tratamento merece atenção especial, principalmente entre pacientes que precisam utilizar medicamentos para prevenir a formação de coágulos. A interrupção ou o uso irregular, sem orientação médica, pode comprometer a eficácia do tratamento e aumentar os riscos à saúde.

Por isso, a participação dos familiares e cuidadores também faz diferença nesse processo, ajudando o paciente a seguir as recomendações e a manter os cuidados necessários em casa.

A conscientização também aborda os cuidados necessários após a alta e a importância de seguir o tratamento indicado — Foto: Divulgação/Hospital São José

Os sintomas geralmente aparecem de forma súbita. Fique atento a:

Alteração na fala - Dificuldade para falar ou compreender, ou fala arrastada.

Boca torta - Um lado do rosto pode ficar caído ao sorrir.

Perda de força - Fraqueza ou dormência em um braço, perna ou lado do corpo.

Alterações na visão - Perda ou mudança súbita da visão.

Tontura e desequilíbrio - Dificuldade repentina para caminhar ou coordenar os movimentos.

SAMU 192 - Suspeitou de um AVC? Ligue imediatamente para o SAMU. Não espere os sintomas passarem. Se possível, anote o horário em que começaram.

Dra. Cassiana Mazon Fraga - Diretora Técnica CRM - 9170 RQE - 6411/ 6382/ 8703

articles.title: Pacientes ficam sem consultas após falha de comunicação no HC  | G1
articles.standfirst: Ponto facultativo referente ao Dia do Servidor Público, celebrado no dia 28 de outubro, foi transferido pelo Governo de Minas Gerais para esta sexta-feira (30). Pacientes alegam que não foram avisados.
articles.summary: Erro de comunicação sobre ponto facultativo no Hospital das Clínicas faz pacientes viajarem até à capital mineira
articles.body:
Pacientes que estavam com consultas e exames marcados no Hospital das Clínicas da UFMG, em Belo Horizonte , não receberam atendimento nesta sexta-feira (30). O local está aberto apenas para urgência e emergência em meio à transferência do ponto facultativo referente ao Dia do Servidor Público.

Celebrado anualmente no dia 28 de outubro, neste ano, o Governo de Minas Gerais transferiu a data conforme com a Portaria MGI nº 8.821, publicada no Diário Oficial da União. No entanto, segundo pacientes, não houve aviso prévio sobre a situação ou contato para remarcações.

A Patrícia Santos, foi uma das pessoas surpreendidas. Moradora de Pará de Minas, no Centro-Oeste de Minas, ela percorreu quase 100 quilômetros até Belo Horizonte em uma van com outros pacientes para fazer um exame de sangue.

“Eu saí às 3h30 da manhã e meu ônibus saiu 4h30 do ponto de encontro. Cheguei aqui por volta de umas 6h50. [...] Como que eu vou sair de Pará de Minas se aqui não tiver uma consulta agendada? É a falta de comunicação”, afirmou.

A acompanhante de uma idosa de 92 anos relata que também não houve comunicação prévia por parte da equipe médica.

"Ela estava marcada para o geriatra agora às 10 horas da manhã. Aí nós chegamos aqui e está fechado. Só que eles não ligaram para poder avisar. Eles tem o meu contato e tem o contato da filha dela", disse Joyce Silva.

Em nota, o Hospital das Clínicas da UFMG, informou que os pacientes teriam sido previamente comunicados por telefone, e-mail e mensagens via WhatsApp. No entanto, reconheceu que “é possível que alguns usuários não tenham sido efetivamente alcançados pelos canais de contato disponíveis”.

A instituição lamentou ocorrido e afirmou que as consultas e exames já foram remarcados pelas equipes assistenciais.

articles.title: Julgamento de empresário que dirigia Porsche e matou trabalhador de aplicativo teve mudanças de versão e divergências em depoimentos; veja | G1
articles.standfirst: Fernando Sastre admitiu ter consumido álcool antes de dirigir, após negar ingestão de bebida em declarações anteriores. Empresário foi condenado a 17 anos de prisão.
articles.summary: Fernando Sastre admitiu ter consumido álcool antes de dirigir, após negar ingestão de bebida em declarações anteriores. Empresário foi condenado a 17 anos de prisão.
articles.body:
O julgamento de Fernando Sastre de Andrade Filho , motorista do Porsche envolvido no acidente que matou o motorista de aplicativo Ornaldo da Silva Viana , em março de 2024, teve mudanças de versão do réu e divergências entre os depoimentos de testemunhas e os argumentos apresentados pela defesa.

O empresário foi condenado a 17 anos, 1 mês e 10 dias de prisão, em regime inicialmente fechado , por homicídio com dolo eventual e lesão corporal gravíssima. O júri terminou na madrugada desta sexta-feira (30).

Um dos principais pontos discutidos durante o julgamento foi o consumo de bebidas alcoólicas antes do acidente. Após negar anteriormente que tivesse bebido, Sastre admitiu, nesta quinta-feira (29), ter consumido dois drinques à base de uísque antes de dirigir.

Em entrevista ao Fantástico, da TV Globo, em maio de 2024, o empresário havia afirmado que tinha tomado apenas água na noite do acidente (veja vídeo abaixo) .

A seguir, veja quatro pontos discutidos durante o julgamento e as versões apresentadas pelo réu, pela defesa e pelas testemunhas ouvidas pela Justiça.

1 - Ele negou ter bebido, mas confessou durante o julgamento

Em 2024 , durante depoimento à polícia e em entrevista ao Fantástico, Fernando Sastre negou ter consumido bebida alcoólica antes do acidente. A então namorada, Giovanna Pinheiro Silva , também afirmou que ele não havia bebido.

Nos depoimentos de 28 e 29 de outubro de 2026 testemunhas ouvidas no júri, entre elas o amigo Marcus Vinicius Machado Rocha e Juliana Simões, namorada de Marcus na época, disseram que Fernando havia consumido bebidas alcoólicas.

No julgamento de 29 de outubro de 2026 : Fernando admitiu pela primeira vez que bebeu antes de dirigir. Disse no tribunal ter consumido dois drinques à base de uísque. Ao admitir o consumo de álcool, o empresário disse que queria contar a verdade e que não pretendia inventar desculpas.

O promotor Rodolfo Morais questionou a mudança de versão e argumentou que o réu só reconheceu o consumo de álcool diante das provas apresentadas.

Fernando Sastre de Andrade Filho (foto) é o motorista do Porsche envolvido no acidente que matou um motorista por aplicativo. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Jonas Marzagão, advogado de Fernando, diz que seu cliente é o único motorista envolvido em um acidente com morte que segue preso em São Paulo .

"Todos os reús nos casos similares estão respondendo em liberdade, inclusive com teste de bafômetro comprovando o uso do bebida alcoólica, e fuga do local de acidente. O que não aconteceu no caso de Fernando. Ele não fez o bafômetro na ocasião porque a polícia não tinha o aparelho para fazer no momento", falou Marzagão.

"Fernando não pediu socorro porque outras pessoas haviam telefonado e pedido, enquanto era retirado do carro. Mas ele ainda permaneceu no local do acidente até ser liberado pelas autoridades", completou o advogado.

2 - Fernando não foi ao hospital para onde disse que seria levado

Outra divergência do julgamento foi sobre a saída de Sastre do local do acidente. A defesa sustentou, logo após a morte do motorista de aplicativo, que Fernando não havia fugido.

A versão era de que ele tinha sido liberado pelos policiais militares para receber atendimento médico, depois que sua mãe chegou ao local. O que foi comprovado pelas câmeras corporais dos policiais envolvidos na ocorrência.

A mãe de Fernando havia informado aos policiais que o levaria ao Hospital São Luiz Ibirapuera. Os policiais militares procuraram o empresário na unidade, mas receberam a informação de que ele não havia dado entrada no hospital.

Na sequência, Fernando e a mãe não atenderam às ligações dos policiais. Ele só se apresentou à delegacia mais de 30 horas depois do acidente.

Durante o julgamento, Daniela Andrade apresentou outra explicação: disse que, antes de ir ao hospital, passou em casa com o filho para que os dois tomassem banho e trocassem de roupa.

Afirmou também que tomou um medicamento para se acalmar, ficou dopada e não conseguiu dirigir. Segundo ela, só levou o filho para fazer exames uma semana depois. A versão também foi apresentada por Fernando Sastre na entrevista que ele deu ao Fantástico , em maio de 2024.

No segundo dia do júri, a policial militar Daisy Romão afirmou que se sentiu enganada pela mãe do empresário, porque acreditava que ela o levaria ao hospital.

3 - A defesa tentou atribuir o acidente a falha mecânica no Porsche

A defesa de Fernando Sastre também apresentou durante o julgamento uma perícia particular que apontou possíveis problemas mecânicos no Porsche envolvido no acidente.

No segundo dia do júri, o perito Alfredo Vieira, contratado pela defesa, apresentou suas conclusões sobre o veículo. Segundo ele, havia indícios de falhas técnicas, incluindo um possível problema na câmera dianteira que poderia comprometer o funcionamento do sistema de alerta de colisão.

Os advogados também exibiram uma animação para apresentar sua interpretação sobre a dinâmica do acidente.

A perícia oficial do Instituto de Criminalística (IC), por sua vez, concluiu que o Porsche trafegava a aproximadamente 156 km/h momentos antes da colisão . O limite de velocidade no trecho da Avenida Salim Farah Maluf onde ocorreu o acidente era de 50 km/h.

Durante o julgamento, a defesa argumentou que possíveis falhas no veículo deveriam ser consideradas na análise das circunstâncias do acidente.

Já a acusação sustentou que a velocidade do Porsche, associada ao consumo de álcool e aos relatos das testemunhas, demonstrava que o empresário havia assumido o risco de provocar uma morte.

4 - Discussão sobre homicídio doloso e culposo

Uma das principais questões analisadas pelos jurados foi se Fernando Sastre assumiu o risco de provocar a morte de Ornaldo Viana ao dirigir o Porsche nas circunstâncias relatadas durante o julgamento.

A defesa, representada pelo advogado Jonas Marzagão, sustentou que o empresário não teve intenção de matar e pediu a desclassificação da acusação para homicídio culposo, modalidade em que não há intenção nem assunção do risco de provocar a morte.

A acusação, por outro lado, defendeu a condenação por homicídio com dolo eventual, quando o autor assume o risco de produzir o resultado.

Durante o julgamento, Marcus Vinicius Machado Rocha, amigo de infância de Sastre e passageiro do Porsche no momento do acidente, afirmou que o empresário havia consumido bebidas alcoólicas e que amigos tentaram convencê-lo a não dirigir.

Marcus também confirmou que Giovanna Pinheiro Silva, então namorada de Fernando, se recusou a entrar no veículo em razão da situação do empresário. Ele próprio, no entanto, decidiu acompanhar o amigo.

Marcus tinha 22 anos e era estudante de medicina na época do acidente. Com o impacto, sofreu fraturas em quatro costelas e precisou passar por uma cirurgia para retirada do baço.

Ele permaneceu cerca de dez dias internado, parte desse período na Unidade de Terapia Intensiva (UTI), e voltou a ser hospitalizado posteriormente por complicações relacionadas à cirurgia.

Marcus Vinicius Machado Rocha diz que Sastre ingeriu álcool antes de dirigir — Foto: Kléber Tomaz/g1

Ao final do julgamento, os jurados reconheceram o dolo eventual na morte de Ornaldo Viana e também condenaram Sastre por lesão corporal gravíssima em relação aos ferimentos sofridos por Marcus.

Na sentença, a juíza mencionou os relatos de que o empresário havia sido advertido por amigos para não dirigir antes do acidente.

O julgamento começou na quarta-feira (28), no Fórum Criminal da Barra Funda, na Zona Oeste de São Paulo. Ao todo, 14 testemunhas foram arroladas no processo, das quais 11 foram ouvidas durante os dois dias de julgamento.

O segundo dia do júri começou por volta das 11h desta quinta-feira. Duas pessoas foram ouvidas no começo: a policial militar Daisy Aparecida Cardoso Romão, que liberou Fernando do local do acidente sem que ele fizesse o teste do bafômetro, e o perito criminal Alfredo Vieira das Neves, contratado pela família do empresário.

Sastre também foi ouvido e admitiu, pela primeira vez, ter ingerido bebida alcoólica no dia em que bateu no carro do motorista de aplicativo (veja mais abaixo).

Durante o depoimento, a policial militar afirmou que foi enganada pela mãe de Fernando. Segundo Daisy, a mulher disse que levaria o filho para receber atendimento médico por causa de um pequeno sangramento no nariz, mas os dois foram para casa.

Fernando Sastre Filho — Foto: Jornal Nacional/Reprodução

Segundo Daisy, a mãe do empresário pediu autorização para levá-lo ao hospital. A policial afirmou que permitiu a saída porque o Samu já havia deixado o local e não havia atendimento médico disponível naquele momento. Questionada sobre a presença dos bombeiros, confirmou que eles ainda estavam na ocorrência.

A policial disse que Fernando estava confuso, mas não afirmou que ele aparentava estar alcoolizado. Ela também declarou que não solicitou escolta para acompanhar o deslocamento até o hospital.

Após a saída, um policial militar, que trabalhava com Daisy, telefonou para a mãe do empresário porque Fernando não havia sido encontrado no Hospital São Luiz para onde ela disse que o levaria. A mulher indicou outra unidade de saúde, mas eles também não foram localizados no local.

Questionada sobre o motivo de ter liberado o empresário sem o teste do bafômetro, Daisy inicialmente não respondeu e depois afirmou que a equipe não tinha um etilômetro na viatura. Ela disse não se lembrar se a carteira de habilitação de Fernando foi recolhida.

MP pede investigação contra perito contratado pela família

O segundo depoimento foi o do perito criminal Alfredo Vieira das Neves, contratado pela família de Fernando Sastre para fazer uma análise técnica do acidente.

Durante a apresentação, ele tentou justificar a colisão com base em imagens do acidente e levantou a possibilidade de falhas no Porsche.

O assistente técnico do Ministério Público questionou o perito sobre o uso de imagens que, na avaliação da acusação, seriam divergentes das utilizadas na análise particular. O Ministério Público também pediu a instauração de um inquérito para apurar suspeita de falsidade ideológica.

A juíza indeferiu o pedido por entender que não cabia a ela determinar a instauração da investigação naquele momento, mas ao próprio Ministério Público. Após a decisão, o órgão anunciou que instauraria o inquérito contra o perito.

Ao responder às perguntas encaminhadas pelos jurados, Alfredo foi questionado se o acidente teria sido evitado caso o Porsche estivesse dentro do limite de velocidade da via. Ele respondeu que, quanto menor a velocidade, menor o risco de acidente.

Durante o depoimento, a PM afirmou que foi enganada pela mãe de Fernando. No dia do crime, a mulher disse à policial que iria levar o filho ferido para o hospital, porém eles foram para casa.

O empresário Fernando Sastre de Andrade Filho, dono do Porsche azul, admitiu nesta quinta-feira (29), pela primeira vez, ter ingerido bebida alcoólica no dia em que bateu no carro do motorista de aplicativo.

Antes, o empresário negava ter consumido álcool naquela noite e afirmava que só tinha bebido água. No início de sua fala no júri, Fernando disse:

"Eu poderia inventar mil desculpas, mas estou aqui entregue a esse plenário, eu acredito na Justiça. Hoje quero dizer a verdade".

Sastre ainda pediu para esclarecer que "jamais foi indiferente" ao ocorrido. "Eu sofro muito com isso até hoje", disse, chorando. Depois afirmou que nunca queria ter provocado aquele acidente. E que queria aproveitar o momento para "pedir com todo respeito, perdão para as vítimas, para as famílias".

"Confesso, sim, que, no dia dos fatos, eu ingeri bebida alcoólica".

O réu ainda lamentou ter provocado o acidente que matou Ornaldo: "Eu imagino toda dor e sofrimento que eles estão sentindo. O seu Ornaldo tinha quase a mesma idade do meu pai. Posso imaginar o que eles estão sentido e toda a devastação".

articles.title: Paciente que casou em hospital conheceu esposa em torneio de futebol | G1
articles.standfirst: Casal se conheceu durante uma partida de futebol na zona rural de Poconé, se casaram na igreja em 1998 e agora esperam a chegada do primeiro neto.
articles.summary: Casal se conheceu  durante uma partida de futebol na zona rural de Poconé, se casaram na igreja em 1998 e agora esperam a chegada do primeiro neto.
articles.body:
Um torneio de futebol na zona rural de Poconé (MT) marcou o início da história de amor entre Deoclides Marques de Arruda , de 56 anos, e Olene Martinha de Souza , de 48 anos. Juntos há 28 anos, os dois realizaram o sonho de se casar no civil durante uma cerimônia no Hospital de Câncer de Mato Grosso (HCanMT), em Cuiabá , nessa segunda-feira (26), onde Deoclides está internado e recebe cuidados paliativos .

Ao g1 , Olene contou que Deoclides jogava pelo time da comunidade Rodeio, onde ela passava as férias escolares todos os anos. Os dois se conheceram ainda na adolescência, durante uma das partidas a que ela foi assistir .

Após seis anos de namoro, eles se casaram em julho de 1998, mas apenas em uma cerimônia religiosa.

Deoclides Marques de Arruda e Olene Martinha de Souza se casaram em uma cerimônia religiosa em 1998 e se casaram no civil em 2026 — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Em 2000, nasceu a filha do casal, Laís Vitória, de 25 anos, que está grávida do primeiro filho. Com isso, os dois aguardam a chegada do primeiro neto.

Olene Martinha de Souza, Deoclides Marques de Arruda e a filha deles, Laís Vitória, de 25 anos — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

No entanto, em abril de 2023, a vida dos dois mudou quando Deoclides foi diagnosticado com câncer no estômago . Ele passou por sessões de quimioterapia e por uma cirurgia para tratar a doença. Em 2026, porém, o câncer voltou.

“Deoclides não é apenas o homem que conheci naquela comunidade. Ele é meu companheiro de vida, o homem com quem construí minha família, o pai da nossa filha e a pessoa com quem compartilhei sonhos, alegrias, dificuldades e tantos anos de caminhada”, disse.

Deoclides Marques de Arruda e Olene Martinha de Souza celebraram o casamento no Hospital do Câncer de Mato Grosso — Foto: Bruno Sampaio Ricci

Cerimônia foi realizada após mobilização de profissionais, voluntários e parceiros — Foto: Bruno Sampaio Ricci

Olene e Deoclides já haviam se casado na Igreja Católica, em 1998, mas ainda sonhavam em oficializar a união no civil. A cerimônia estava prevista para ocorrer em Poconé, onde vivem, mas a internação dele impediu que os planos fossem realizados na cidade.

A equipe do hospital organizou a cerimônia em dois dias, com a ajuda de voluntários e empresas parceiras. A mobilização começou depois que Deoclides manifestou o desejo de oficializar a união com a companheira.

Profissionais de diferentes setores do hospital e parceiros voluntários contribuíram com itens e serviços para o casamento, como terno, alianças, música e vestido de noiva. Familiares e amigos também acompanharam a cerimônia.
